question: what is reg s-p?
answer: Reg S-P is an SEC rule (17 CFR 248.30) that governs how financial firms handle customers' nonpublic personal information. The part relevant to this session, mentioned back on slide 5, is the requirement that firms have written policies "reasonably designed to require oversight, including through due diligence and monitoring, of service providers." So if a broker-dealer, investment adviser, or similar regulated firm wants to send client data to an LLM provider, Reg S-P means they can't just do it casually — they need to vet that provider and keep monitoring it, similar in spirit to how HIPAA requires a BAA for health data. It's the finance-sector analog to the healthcare requirement, showing that this "sign a contract, oversee the vendor" approach isn't just good practice but is often a legal obligation.

question: what is a baa?
answer: A BAA is a Business Associate Agreement, required under HIPAA whenever protected health information (PHI) is going to be handled by an outside vendor — in this context, an LLM provider. It's a specific legal contract, distinct from a general Data Processing Agreement, that binds the vendor to HIPAA's rules for safeguarding PHI: things like how the data can be used, security requirements, and breach notification. Slide 5 quotes the actual regulation on this — 45 CFR 164.502(e) — which says "satisfactory assurances" must be documented through a written contract meeting the requirements in §164.504(e). So practically, if you're a healthcare business and want to send patient data to a model provider, you can't rely just on the standard DPA; you need that provider to also sign a BAA, and as slide 3 notes, that's available as part of the standard commercial API account for the major providers, or as slide 4 shows, you can get it via your existing cloud provider's HIPAA BAA if you run the model on AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud.

question: when does a healthcare firm need a baa
answer:
A healthcare firm needs a BAA whenever it shares protected health information (PHI) with an outside vendor who will handle, process, or have access to that data — which includes sending PHI to an LLM provider. The trigger isn't really about size or context beyond that: if PHI is going to leave the firm's own walls to a third party like a model provider, HIPAA requires that written contract be in place first, per 45 CFR 164.502(e).

So concretely, from this session's framing: if a healthcare business wants to use an LLM on patient data — say, summarizing clinical notes or answering questions about a patient record — they need the BAA before any of that PHI touches the model provider's API. As slide 3 notes, this is available as an add-on to the standard commercial API account. And as slide 4 discusses, if their data already lives on AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud, they can get HIPAA coverage through the cloud provider's own BAA by running the model natively on that cloud (Bedrock, Vertex AI, Azure Foundry), avoiding the need for a separate agreement with the model company as a distinct party.

One nuance the session doesn't spell out but is worth knowing: if the data is properly de-identified per HIPAA's Safe Harbor or Expert Determination standards, it's no longer considered PHI, and a BAA isn't required. But that de-identification has to meet HIPAA's specific technical bar — just removing a name isn't enough — so in practice, if there's any doubt, firms treat it as PHI and get the BAA.

question: If the agent only has read-only access, how can a prompt injection steal our rate table?
answer: Good question — read-only stops the destructive actions we listed earlier (deleting, corrupting, overwriting), but it doesn't stop reading. If the agent's job is to read the rate table and it's read-only, it can still see the data; the danger is what happens after it reads. If that same agent also has any outbound channel — it can render a URL, fetch a web page, send an email, or produce a document that later phones home — an injection can instruct it to smuggle the rate table out through that channel, exactly like EchoLeak. Copilot didn't need write access to your mailbox to leak data; it just needed to read private content and have a way to push data out via a URL. So read-only access closes the "destructive action" leg but does nothing about the "outbound channel" leg of the lethal trifecta. To actually stop exfiltration you need to remove or restrict the outbound channel itself — no web rendering, no email sending, whitelisted recipients, sanitized output — not just make the data access read-only.
